Spiritual Adultery
SPIR-ih-choo-ul uh-DUL-ter-ee
noun phrase (unfaithfulness to God)
From the prophetic figure that likens idolatry and worldliness to marital infidelity; God the husband of His covenant people, who play the harlot when they forsake Him.

Biblical Definition

Spiritual adultery is the unfaithfulness of God's covenant people when they forsake Him for other lovers—idols, false gods, or the world—a sin Scripture portrays under the figure of marital infidelity. The LORD is the husband of His people; Israel is the wife of His covenant; and her idolatry is adultery against Him. So the prophets cry: “Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel”; and Ezekiel laments the wife that committeth adultery, taking strangers instead of her husband. Hosea was commanded to take a wife of whoredoms as a living parable of the land that had committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD. The New Testament carries the figure to the heart: “Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God.” The dictionary marks spiritual adultery as a sin of the affections, not merely of outward act: it is the heart that loves and trusts and serves another in the place that belongs to God alone. Every idol, whether of wood or of the heart—money, pleasure, reputation, self—is a rival lover, and to embrace it is to break covenant with the divine Husband. The doctrine deepens the seriousness of idolatry and worldliness by setting them in the language of betrayed love; and it magnifies the grace of God, who, like Hosea redeeming his faithless wife, woos back His adulterous people and says, I will betroth thee unto me for ever.

Webster 1828 Definition

The unfaithfulness of God's covenant people when they forsake Him for idols or the world (Jeremiah 3:20; James 4:4); idolatry and worldliness portrayed as marital infidelity against the divine Husband, a sin of the affections, not merely of act.

SPIRITUAL ADULTERY, noun phrase. Unfaithfulness to God, who is the husband of His covenant people, by turning to idols or the world.

Israel deals treacherously with the LORD as a wife departing from her husband (Jeremiah 3:20).

Hosea's marriage figures the land that committed whoredom, departing from the LORD (Hosea 1:2).

“The friendship of the world is enmity with God” (James 4:4).

A sin of the affections: loving, trusting, or serving another in God's place.

Key Scripture

Jas 4:4 — "Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God."

Jer 3:20 — "Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD."

Eze 16:32 — "But as a wife that committeth adultery, which taketh strangers instead of her husband!"

Ho 1:2 — "The beginning of the word of the LORD by Hosea. And the LORD said to Hosea, Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the trivializing of idolatry and worldliness, so that the believer's flirtation with the world is no longer felt as betrayal of a covenant Husband.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gravity of worldliness as covenant infidelity. The modern believer easily regards friendship with the world as harmless and idolatry as a primitive sin of statues, feeling no betrayal in loving money, pleasure, or self. The prophets and the apostle James forbid this complacency: to befriend the world is to commit adultery against God, who is the Husband of His people. The figure of marital betrayal restores the seriousness; the heart that gives to a rival what belongs to God alone has broken covenant with its Lord.

The doctrine also magnifies the astonishing grace of God toward His unfaithful people. Hosea was commanded to redeem his adulterous wife, a living parable of the LORD who pursues His faithless bride, betroths her again unto Himself in righteousness, and heals her backsliding. The dictionary holds both edges: spiritual adultery is real betrayal, to be repented of with shame; and the divine Husband is full of mercy, calling His wandering people home. The remedy is not lighter views of the sin but a heart wholly restored to its first love, that the believer cleave to the Lord and renounce every rival lover.

Hebrew Roots

From the prophetic marriage-figure: God the husband, His people the wife, and idolatry the zenunim (whoredoms) of an unfaithful spouse; the Greek moichalis (adulteress) is James's word for the worldly church.

expand to see more

Zanah, Hebrew, to commit fornication or play the harlot, used of Israel's idolatry.

Zenunim, Hebrew, “whoredoms,” the prophetic term for covenant unfaithfulness.

Moichalis, Greek, an adulteress, James's address to the world-loving church.

The marriage-covenant figure casts the LORD as husband and His people as wife.

Hosea's marriage enacts the parable of God's faithless yet redeemed bride.

Usage

"The pastor named the love of the world as spiritual adultery, a betrayal of the covenant Husband."

"He preached Hosea to show the grace that redeems even an adulterous bride."

"She repented of the idols of her heart, seeing them as rival lovers against her Lord."
